guide.title: Bay Ridge, Brooklyn: Yellow Hook, Shore Road, the Narrows
guide.intro: Bay Ridge was part of the town of New Utrecht, formally established by Dutch settlers in 1657, on land where European settlement dates to the 1636 purchase of 936 acres by Willem Adriaenszen Bennett and Jacques Bentyn. The area held two villages, Yellow Hook to the north and Fort Hamilton to the south. In December 1853 residents changed the northern name to Bay Ridge to shed the association with yellow fever. Country estates went up along Shore Road as the area became a rural summer resort in the mid-1800s, and a building boom followed in 1902-1903. The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, opened on November 21, 1964, cut through the southern end of it and displaced roughly 7,500 residents.

sections.heading: Estates, Norwegians and the bridge
sections.body:
The ridge above the Narrows drew country estates. Henry C. Murphy acquired the Owl's Head property in 1856 and built there; the industrialist Eliphalet Williams Bliss expanded it, and after Bliss died in 1903 his will let the city buy the land cheaply. The city purchased it in 1928, the estate structures were gone by 1940, and waterfront portions were later lost to a wastewater treatment plant built in 1952.

By 1971 Bay Ridge held what was described as the fourth-largest Norwegian city in the world, with about 55,000 Norwegian residents; Eighth Avenue was nicknamed Lapskaus Boulevard after the stew, and a Leif Ericson statue donated by Crown Prince Olav was installed in 1939. As of 2023 roughly 30,000 residents of Norwegian descent remained, and the Norwegian Constitution Day parade is held on Third Avenue each year. The New York Times has called Bay Ridge the heart of Brooklyn's Arab community, alongside longstanding Irish, Italian, Greek, Russian, Polish and other Eastern European populations.

The Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge was designed by Othmar Ammann, Leopold Just and colleagues at Ammann & Whitney and built between August 1959 and November 1964 at a cost of $320 million. Residents lobbied for a Belt Parkway approach; the Board of Estimate approved the Seventh Avenue route in December 1958 over their objections. The Brooklyn approach displaced roughly 7,500 people and required demolishing the island fortification of Fort Lafayette.

In 2007 an EF2 tornado with winds of 111 to 135 miles per hour struck near 68th Street and Bay Ridge Avenue, damaging eleven houses and deforesting about 40 percent of Leif Ericson Park.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The R is Bay Ridge's subway. Bay Ridge Avenue and 77th Street are in the neighborhood; 86th Street sits on the border of Bay Ridge and Fort Hamilton. The line's southern terminal, Bay Ridge-95th Street, is at Fourth Avenue and 95th Street in Fort Hamilton.

NYC Ferry calls at the 69th Street Pier, the American Veterans Memorial Pier. Service began there on the South Brooklyn route in June 2017, and the St. George route took over Bay Ridge service in 2025.

sections.heading: The shore
sections.body:
Shore Road carries a strip of parkland, Shore Road Park, and the Narrows Botanical Gardens, which have been running since 1995, sit on it between Bay Ridge Avenue and 72nd Street. Owl's Head Park, about 24 acres on a glacial moraine, has harbor views, a skate park, a dog run, playgrounds, a spray pool, basketball courts and a hill people sled on in winter. At 69th Street the American Veterans Memorial Pier carries a September 11 memorial light sculpture and doubles as the ferry landing.

Inland, several groups of houses carry designations: the Senator Street Historic District, forty Neo-Renaissance brownstone rowhouses of 1906-1912 by Fred W. Eisenla, listed on the National Register on October 10, 2002; the houses at 216-264 Ovington Avenue, listed in 2007; the fifty-four rowhouses of Doctors' Row, on Bay Ridge Parkway between 4th and 5th Avenues, designated a New York City historic district in 2019; and two individual New York City landmarks, the 1847 Bennett-Farrell-Feldman House and the 1917 house at 8200 Narrows Avenue that everyone calls the Gingerbread House.

faq.question: How do I get to Bay Ridge?
faq.answer: The R serves Bay Ridge Avenue and 77th Street in the neighborhood, and 86th Street on the border of Bay Ridge and Fort Hamilton; the line's southern terminal, Bay Ridge-95th Street, is at Fourth Avenue and 95th Street in Fort Hamilton. NYC Ferry calls at the 69th Street Pier, where the St. George route took over Bay Ridge service in 2025.

faq.question: Why is it called Bay Ridge?
faq.answer: The northern of the two villages here was called Yellow Hook. In December 1853 residents changed the name to Bay Ridge to shed the association with yellow fever.

faq.question: What happened to Fort Lafayette?
faq.answer: The island fortification was demolished to make way for the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge's Brooklyn anchorage. The bridge opened on November 21, 1964, and its approach displaced roughly 7,500 Bay Ridge residents.

faq.question: What is the Gingerbread House?
faq.answer: The house at 8200 Narrows Avenue, built in 1917 to designs by James Sarsfield Kennedy and designated a New York City landmark. It is a private residence, so it is an exterior to look at rather than a site to enter.

faq.question: Where can I eat in Bay Ridge?
faq.answer: Tanoreen, at 7523 3rd Avenue, serves Palestinian home cooking and other dishes of the Levant. Its chef, Rawia Bishara, grew up in Nazareth.

faq.question: Is there a cinema in Bay Ridge?
faq.answer: Alpine Cinemas at 6817 5th Avenue is a working multiplex with RealD 3D screens and open-caption screenings of selected titles; Screen 8 has stadium reclining seating.

places.name: Owl's Head Park
places.address: 68th Street and Colonial Road, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: About 24 acres on a glacial moraine with harbor views, a skate park, a dog run, playgrounds, a spray pool, basketball courts and a hill people sled on in winter.
places.history: The site was settled first by the Canarsee people and then by Dutch colonists in the seventeenth century. Henry C. Murphy acquired the property in 1856 and built an estate; the industrialist Eliphalet Williams Bliss expanded it, and after Bliss died in 1903 his will let the city acquire it cheaply. The city purchased it in 1928, the estate structures were gone by 1940, and waterfront portions were later lost to a wastewater treatment plant built in 1952.

places.name: Narrows Botanical Gardens
places.address: Shore Road between Bay Ridge Avenue and 72nd Street, Brooklyn, NY 11209
places.summary: A volunteer-run nonprofit garden on Shore Road, operating since 1995, holding a Turtle & Wildlife Sanctuary, a Native Plant Garden and Betty's Pollinator Garden. It runs plant sales, an Earth Day celebration, a lavender harvest and tree-pit restoration projects.

places.name: Shore Road Park
places.summary: A park running along Shore Road. New York Road Runners hosts a weekly open run here.

places.name: American Veterans Memorial Pier (69th Street Pier)
places.address: 69th Street at the waterfront, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: The pier at the foot of 69th Street, carrying a September 11 memorial light sculpture and serving as the NYC Ferry landing for Bay Ridge.

places.name: Leif Ericson Park
places.address: Between 66th and 67th Streets along Fort Hamilton Parkway, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: The park where Bay Ridge's Norwegian Constitution Day celebration is held, holding a Leif Ericson statue donated by Crown Prince Olav of Norway and installed in 1939. About 40 percent of its trees were lost in the 2007 tornado.

places.name: Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge
places.summary: The suspension bridge linking Bay Ridge to Staten Island, opened on November 21, 1964. It is best treated as something to look at rather than a site to visit.
places.history: Othmar Ammann, Leopold Just and colleagues at Ammann & Whitney designed it. Construction ran from August 1959 to November 1964 at a cost of $320 million. The Brooklyn approach displaced roughly 7,500 Bay Ridge residents and required the demolition of the island fortification Fort Lafayette; residents had lobbied unsuccessfully for a Belt Parkway approach instead of the Seventh Avenue route the Board of Estimate approved in December 1958.

places.name: Alpine Cinemas
places.summary: A working multiplex cinema with RealD 3D projection and kid-sized 3D glasses for children aged 8 and under, and open-caption screenings of selected titles. Screen 8 has stadium reclining seating. Wednesday tickets are $6.00 all day, with a $2 surcharge for 3D.

places.name: 8200 Narrows Avenue House (Gingerbread House)
places.summary: A 1917 residence designed by James Sarsfield Kennedy and designated a New York City landmark. It is a private house, so the exterior is what there is to see.

places.name: Bennett-Farrell-Feldman House
places.summary: Built in 1847 at 119 95th Street and designated a New York City individual landmark on August 3, 1999. An accompanying outbuilding, thought to have been used as a barn, could not be saved and was demolished. Local legend holds that the house was rotated so its widow's walk would no longer face the Narrows.

places.name: Senator Street Historic District
places.summary: Forty Neo-Renaissance brownstone rowhouses built between 1906 and 1912 by the architect Fred W. Eisenla, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on October 10, 2002.

places.name: Houses at 216-264 Ovington Avenue
places.summary: The rowhouses at 216-264 Ovington Avenue, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 5, 2007 under reference number 07000488.

places.name: Tanoreen
places.summary: A restaurant serving Palestinian home cooking and other dishes of the Levant — Syria, Jordan and Lebanon. Its chef, Rawia Bishara, grew up in Nazareth. Dishes named in an independent review include fetti, musakhan, knafeh and baba ghanoush.
